claims.text: Lattice-distortion-induced dislocation pinning is the dominant mechanism governing hardness and strength in high-entropy alloys.
Increased atomic-size mismatch creates local strain fields.
Local strain fields generated by atomic-size mismatch inhibit dislocation motion.
Composition can be varied systematically to change atomic-size mismatch while other processing parameters are held constant.
Identical thermal histories and processing routes can isolate the effect of atomic-size mismatch from other strengthening contributions.
Localized lattice distortions generate strain fields and dislocation-pinning sites.
A higher degree of atomic-size mismatch causes greater lattice distortion.
Greater lattice distortion increases strain-field density.
The resulting strain fields act as obstacles to dislocation motion.
Obstruction of dislocation motion raises the barrier to plastic deformation.
A higher barrier to plastic deformation increases hardness and yield strength.
Alloys with higher atomic-size mismatch will have greater hardness than a minimal-mismatch baseline alloy.
Alloys with higher atomic-size mismatch will have greater yield strength than a minimal-mismatch baseline alloy.
TEM will reveal a higher density of pinned dislocations in high-mismatch alloys than in minimal-mismatch alloys.
Minimizing atomic-size mismatch leads to lower lattice distortion and reduced dislocation pinning.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply to single-phase concentrated solid-solution high-entropy alloys.
Precipitation hardening, grain-boundary effects, or secondary-phase formation may mask or invalidate the proposed relationship.
The quantitative contribution of lattice distortion relative to grain-size refinement and work hardening is uncertain.
Synergistic effects in multielement systems may complicate simple correlations between atomic-size mismatch and mechanical properties.
